paper_title: Build, Don't Play: Self-Improving LLM Research Agents Develop a Hearthstone Battlegrounds AI That Rivals Top Players

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Can LLM agents carry a hard real-world problem from raw data to a system that holds its own against people? We study this in Hearthstone Battlegrounds, an eight-player auto-battler with stochastic shops and battles, hidden information and nearly a thousand interacting cards. We present AutoTavern, a self-improving research system: specialised LLM research agents share a typed research memory, every claim passes verification gates, and live games close the loop, so the agents improve the simulator, opponents and policy and, from the same feedback, their own research process; a human sets goals and rules on ambiguous mechanics. In 20 days AutoTavern built TavernGym, the first faithful, full-content reproduction of the live game, and delivered 23 versions of TavernAgent, trained with PPO against opponents calibrated to real games. TavernAgent plays complete games on the live ladder by itself: its rating rose from 6,000 to about 15,000 and, on the public leaderboard's measure, its last 20 records average a placement of 1.60 with 80% first places, better than the server's ten highest-rated players on every statistic (2.34, 59%). TavernBench, 960 tasks in 40 scenarios, shows that the system the agents built is the strongest player: TavernAgent answers 91% of the play tasks against at most 63% for frontier LLMs, and decides in 0.03 s where they need up to 26 s; within the second a live turn allows, it keeps 90% and no LLM more than 26%. LLM agents build far better than they play. We will open-source TavernBench and TavernGym at https://github.com/MCG-NJU/AutoTavern.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: Games have long served as milestones for artificial intelligence, from Go and chess [Silver et al., 2016, 2018] to StarCraft II, Dota 2, poker, Mahjong and Stratego [Vinyals et al., 2019, Berner et al., 2019, Brown and Sandholm, 2019, Li et al., 2020, Perolat et al., 2022]. Each of these systems was the product of large team of human experts who built the environment, designed the learning algorithm and debugged the countless ways in which simulated training world differs from the real game. Today, LLM agents write and run much of the code behind such systems, and growing line of work asks whether they can automate the research itself [Lu et al., 2024, Yamada et al., 2026, Wijk et al., 2025, Srikanth et al., 2026]. Existing evidence, however, comes from benchmark tasks or paper reviews; it remains open whether agents can carry hard, real-world problem from raw data to system that holds its own against people, where performance is ultimately measured in the real game. We study this question in Hearthstone Battlegrounds, Blizzards eight-player auto-battler, played by millions. Each turn player spends gold in randomly stocked tavern to buy, sell and position minions, then fights an automatic battle against one opponent; players are eliminated in turn until one remains. The game combines stochastic shops and battles, hidden information about seven opponents, Figure 1: TAVERNBENCH at glance. (a) Accuracy (%) per capability, with the play score counting only answers within the second live turn allows per decision; numbers: TAVERNAGENT. (b) Play score against seconds per decision; shaded: too slow for live turn. All systems are in Table 4. shared card pool, horizon of hundreds of decisions with reward only at the end, and content base of nearly one thousand interacting cards, heroes and trinkets that changes with every patch. No faithful simulator of the live game has been available, and existing AI work either advises human players or studies simplified versions of the game (Section 2). We present AUTOTAVERN, self-improving research system in which team of specialised LLM research agents iterates model autonomously (Figure 2). Its principle is reality-anchored selfimprovement. Agents for the environment, training, opponent modelling, evaluation and deployment communicate only through typed, versioned research memory; five verification gates stand between every claim and that memory; and live games on the real ladder close the loop, turning discrepancies between simulation and reality into fixes of rules, input encodings and opponent models. The same feedback improves the agents research process: errors they catch become lessons in the memory, loaded by every later session, or new gates, so each iteration starts from better world and better method. Because the loop does not pay for the same mistake twice, it took the agent from its first version to the level of the servers best players in 20 days. The human sets goals and rules on ambiguous mechanics. Over 20 days the framework produced: AUTOTAVERN, self-improving research system in which LLM research agents improve model, its training world and their own research process from the feedback of real environment. In 20 days it ran about 10,000 experiments and delivered 23 agent versions with 418 human messages in all, and the errors it caught became lessons and gates that changed how it works (Sections 4 and 8). TAVERNGYM, the first faithful, full-content reproduction of the live game: all 978 game objects of patch 36.6.3, deterministic, 190280 complete eight-player games per second on single core, and aligned rule by rule with real games (Section 5). We will open-source it. TAVERNAGENT, the first Battlegrounds AI to play complete games on the live ladder, and the strongest. Its 23 successive versions, each passing an evaluation gate, raised the first-place rate against reality-calibrated opponents from 1.9% to 41.5% (random legal play and scripted bot: 0%), and on the live ladder the deployed agent climbed by itself from rating of 6,000 to about 15,000; on the public leaderboards measure its recent results are better than the servers ten highest-rated players on every statistic (Section 6 and Section D). TAVERNBENCH, the first decision benchmark for Battlegrounds: 960 tasks in 40 scenarios across eight categories, labelled by the simulator (Section 7). We will open-source it. 2 Figure 2: Overview of AUTOTAVERN, self-improving research system. Six LLM research agents share one research memory and run three loops: training (minutes), research (hours) and the live ladder (days). The human sets goals, rules on ambiguous mechanics and presses the keys the AI names. Chart: first-place rate of the 23 delivered TAVERNAGENT versions on one simulator build and three unseen seeds (24,576 games per point). The benchmark bears out our title (Figure 1): asked to make the decisions themselves, the LLMs that built ladder-level agent fall well short of the system they built, and decide far too slowly for live turn (Section 7). LLMs build far better than they play.

sections.title: 2 Related Work
sections.content: AI for Hearthstone and Battlegrounds. Research on Hearthstone has focused on the two-player constructed mode [Dockhorn and Mostaghim, 2019]. For Battlegrounds, Zolboot et al. [2022] built Monte Carlo tree search assistant on simplified simulator, evaluated on the first turns of recorded games; an open-source simulator for reinforcement learning omits heroes [Elimelech, 2019]; community tools such as Firestone and Bobs Buddy simulate only the combat phase to show win odds [Zero-to-Heroes, 2017, HSReplay.net, 2020]; and DeepBattler uses an LLM to give players advice during live games without an environment or an agent of its own [William-Dic, 2025]. None reproduces the full live game or trains an agent that plays it  (Table 2)  . Large-scale game RL. Superhuman systems for Go, StarCraft II, Dota 2, Honor of Kings, poker, Mahjong, DouDizhu and Stratego [Silver et al., 2016, Vinyals et al., 2019, Berner et al., 2019, Ye et al., 2020, Brown and Sandholm, 2019, Li et al., 2020, Zha et al., 2021, Perolat et al., 2022] combine self-play or human data with large-scale training and start from an existing environment. We use standard learner, PPO [Schulman et al., 2017] with transformer [Vaswani et al., 2017], and focus on building and correcting the training world itself, which here is done by agents. LLM research agents. The AI Scientist automates idea generation, experiments and paper writing [Lu et al., 2024, Yamada et al., 2025, 2026]; Eureka and AlphaEvolve use LLMs to propose reward functions and programs that an automatic evaluator scores [Ma et al., 2024, Novikov et al., 2025]; 3 MLAgentBench, MLE-bench, RE-Bench and PaperBench measure agents on machine-learning tasks [Huang et al., 2024, Chan et al., 2025, Wijk et al., 2025, Starace et al., 2025]; and recent systems orchestrate coding agents or improve their own scaffolds [Lange et al., 2026, Zhang et al., 2025, Srikanth et al., 2026]; Kirgis et al. [2026] find that agents complete the engineering of open-ended projects but struggle with the research questions. AUTOTAVERN differs in what improves and in how the improvement is judged. Its agents improve their research process through memory of lessons and new verification gates rather than by rewriting their own code. Progress is measured on live ladder against people, reality loop re-anchors simulator and opponents to live games against proxy drift, and verification gates stand between every claim and the shared memory against false findings. LLMs as game players. Benchmarks evaluate LLMs on text, puzzle, video and strategic games [Wu et al., 2024, Duan et al., 2024, Costarelli et al., 2024, Paglieri et al., 2025, Guertler et al., 2025, Hu et al., 2025] and on poker decisions [Zhuang et al., 2025]. TAVERNBENCH adds stochastic multiplayer game of economy and combat with answers verified by simulator, strong specialised agent as reference and real-time view: the decisions model gets right within live turns time.

sections.title: 3 Hearthstone Battlegrounds
sections.content: A game has eight players, each with hero, 3040 health and Hero Power. Every turn consists of recruit phase and combat phase. In the recruit phase the player spends gold (3 on turn 1, rising to 10) to buy minions from tavern of random offers drawn from pool shared by all players, sell minions, refresh or freeze the offers, upgrade the tavern tier (17, unlocking stronger minions), play cards from the hand, use the Hero Power and arrange the warband of up to seven minions. Three copies of minion merge into golden version that offers discovery from the next tier. Battlecries, deathrattles, auras, magnetic attachments, tavern spells, trinkets and other mechanics interact across turns. In combat, the warband fights one opponent automatically, with random targets; the loser takes damage, and players are eliminated until one remains. The outcome is the placement, 1 to 8. We model game as partially observable stochastic game with terminal utility of the placement. player observes its own state and, for each opponent, only the public leaderboard and the warband last seen in combat. The current patch (36.6.3) contains 978 game objects: minions, heroes, trinkets, spells and other cards. game lasts about 15 turns and about 450 atomic actions per player.

sections.title: 4 The AUTOTAVERN System
sections.content: AUTOTAVERN is self-improving research system: LLM research agents improve model against an environment they cannot simulate exactly and, from the same feedback, their own research process. Its central idea is reality-anchored self-improvement: every proxy the agents optimise (the simulator, the opponent model, the exams) is re-anchored to the real game at fixed cadence, every claim must survive check designed to refute it before it changes the shared state, and the errors these checks catch change the process that made them. Problem setting. The research state at iteration is set of artifacts: an environment Et, an opponent model Ot, set of exams Xt and policy πt, together with the research process itself: the memory Mt of findings and lessons and the gates Gt. The goal is the policys real performance J(π), its expected placement on the live ladder, observable only through few slow, costly games. Inside the loop the agents can only improve proxy ˆJ(π; Et, Ot, Xt). Two failure modes follow. Proxy drift: ˆJ improves while does not, because Et or Ot is wrong in way the policy exploits. False findings: reading that reflects noise, leak or selection is recorded as result and steers later work. AUTOTAVERN answers the first with reality loop and the second with verification gates; both act on shared memory, the only channel through which findings pass between agents. Self-improvement closes the loop: an iteration updates the artifacts and, when it catches an error, Mt and Gt, so that later iterations do not repeat it. Role agents. Long-running LLM research agents own the research roles (Figure 2, Table 5). research lead chooses the next problem and dispatches work. An environment agent implements and verifies rules and repairs discrepancies found in live games, and an opponent agent builds human-like opponents from human statistics and live games. training agent designs recipes and curricula, 4 Algorithm 1 One iteration of AUTOTAVERN 1: Observe: read the research memory, the latest evaluations and the latest live games 2: Diagnose: attribute the largest gap to rules, input encoding, opponent model, policy or goal 3: Plan: choose an intervention (fix the environment, recalibrate opponents, change the recipe, add label) 4: Implement: the responsible agent builds it in isolation and passes the test gate 5: Train: register runs; the scheduler executes them and queues successors 6: Evaluate: compare within one build; re-check on unseen seeds; deliver only if better 7: Deploy: the delivered model plays on the live ladder; game records flow back 8: Reflect: record findings, correct earlier conclusions, turn caught errors into lessons and gates an evaluation agent measures, re-checks and audits, and deployment agent maintains the client controller and the models input formats. Short-lived workers run probes and implement features. Typed research memory. Agents never talk directly; they read and write versioned, typed stores: ledger of numbered findings in which correction is new entry pointing back, registry of rule decisions and open questions, hand-over note, an experiment registry, and store of lessons loaded at the start of every session. finding is never edited away, so the memory records how conclusions changed as well as what they are. Verification gates. Five gates stand between an idea and the shared state: G1 build: code change passes the full test suite before it reaches the shared build; G2 contract: every model is tied to the simulator build it was trained on, and the controller refuses model trained for another; G3 comparison: models are compared only within one build, over several seeds; G4 delivery: candidate is delivered only after re-check on seeds it was not selected on; G5 reality: delivered models play the live ladder, and their games are replayed in the simulator. The gates acted throughout: candidates were held back after re-checks, findings were revised by later ones, and live games led to 184 fixes of rules, input encodings, the client controller and the opponents, counted in Section A. Reality loop. The controller logs every live game; game records are linked to the agents decisions; the evaluation agent replays real combats and real recruit steps in TAVERNGYM and reports where simulation and reality part; the responsible agent fixes rules, input encodings or opponents, and the next iteration trains on the corrected world (Section 8). Self-improvement. The loop improves the research process as well as its products. finding that overturns an earlier one is recorded as correction pointing back. mistake the agents trace to their own method becomes lesson that every later session loads at its start, or new gate. Of the six errors in Section 8, two became gates (the re-check on unseen seeds, G4, and the comparison of the two input encoders in G2) and two became standing rules (reseed copied games, and calibrate opponents on those the learner meets). Because caught error changes the process and not only the current result, the loop does not pay for the same mistake twice: over the 20 days the 23 delivered versions raised the first-place rate from 1.9% to 41.5% (Figure 2).

sections.title: 4.2 Autonomy in numbers
sections.content: Table 1 summarises the 20 days. Agents registered about 10,000 experiments, and 23 agent versions passed the delivery gate. The human typed 418 messages over the whole project, 0.6% of all messages. Labelled by their main intent (automatically, checked by hand on sample), 42% ask for progress or report, 24% set or change goal, 11% concern resources, 8% approve proposal, 6% correct an agent, 5% rule on game mechanic and 5% report live games.

sections.title: 5 TAVERNGYM: Reproducing the Real Game
sections.content: Design. TAVERNGYM is Rust engine with thin Python bindings. One effect context serves the recruit and the combat phase, so every card is table of event hooks that work the same in both; the state is an arena of entities, cheap to copy and serialisable; all randomness comes from one seeded generator, so seed and an action sequence reproduce game bit for bit. Card data are generated from the games own files, later patches are overlays, and rule hash identifies every build. Fidelity to the live game. All 978 objects of patch 36.6.3 are implemented. 375 verification records and 220 confirmed rule decisions document how each mechanic was checked, and unit tests, fuzzing with invariant checks after every action and an exact legal-action mask guard the implementation. Live games led to 46 fixes of rules and card data and 73 of input encodings, found by replaying live turns, combats and offers in the engine (Sections and 8). Speed and interface. complete eight-player game with scripted bots takes 3.65.3 ms on one core (190280 games per second), and late-game combat 1319 µs (5276 thousand per second). The RL interface exposes 245 discrete actions with an exact legal mask, player-view observation with only the information visible in the real client, batched environments and exact save and restore of running games for lookahead and replays.

sections.title: 6 TAVERNAGENT: Learning to Play the Live Game
sections.content: Model and training. TAVERNAGENT is an entity transformer: each own minion, hand card, tavern offer, pending choice and opponent is token (up to 56), card is represented by an identity embedding, static features and an embedding of its rule text, and pointer head produces the 245 masked action logits next to value and placement heads (d=384, 8 layers, 8 heads, 18M parameters, the best of three sizes in an early comparison, Table 8). It is trained with PPO [Schulman et al., 2017] on about one million decisions per iteration with terminal placement utility; each training stage of 300 iterations covers about 310 million decisions (570 thousand games) and starts from the previous stage under KL anchor. Reality-calibrated opponents. This was the largest single gain: from the same checkpoint and with the same budget, training against the calibrated libraries raises the first-place rate from 20.9% to 27.2% on the main exam and from 10.3% to 13.5% on the harder one  (Table 3)  . Iterative improvement. The chart in Figure 2 traces all 23 delivered versions (TA-1 to TA-23, Table 6), re-measured on one simulator build, one exam and three unseen seeds: the first-place rate rises from 1.9% to 41.5% and the average placement from 3.40 to 2.33  (Table 3)  . Live ladder. The deployed agent plays the live ranked ladder by itself: the controller feeds the live games state to the policy in the environments own encoding, the policy decides every operation, and human presses the shortcut key the AI names, feature of the games official plug-in (Section D). Most delivered versions entered this loop, so the agents iterations are also its climb on the ladder (Figure 3 and Table 10): over 392 games on days 518 of the project the rating rose from 6,000 to 14,007. Games in which the client failed (96, flagged by the controllers logs, never by the result; Section D) measure the client rather than the agent; without them the average placement is 3.22, with 16.4% first places and 77.1% top-four finishes. sections.title: 7 TAVERNBENCH: Build, Don’t Play
sections.content: Design. TAVERNBENCH asks whether general-purpose LLMs can make the decisions that TAVERNAGENT makes: 960 tasks in 40 scenarios and eight categories  (Table 13)  . task gives the player-visible state as text, the rule text of every card shown, an objective and an answer format. Labels come from TAVERNGYM: rule tasks execute the actions; combat tasks simulate 4,096 combats; short-term decisions are scored by the simulated win rate of the next combat after the chosen option (correct within three points of the best); strategic decisions are turn plans cut from natural games (upgrade, buy, refresh or save the Gold), each played out 128 times by an earlier version (TA-21) and kept when one is better by quarter place and two standard errors; hero and trinket choices are scored against top human players (Section E). TAVERNAGENTs interface. TAVERNAGENT does not read the text: it receives the tasks engine state as in game. Its policy answers the choices judged by playing the game out, its value head the hero offers. Combat questions and short-term decisions use TAVERNGYM as the agents model of the game: it applies each option and simulates 256 combats after it (one-step lookahead). Rule tasks ask what the environment does, which TAVERNGYM answers by construction; TAVERNAGENT is not scored on them, and its row shows dash. Protocol. LLMs answer with one JSON object within fixed output budget, reasoning included (more is scored as wrong), in the fastest mode that answered pilot of one task from each scenario (Section E). All systems answer the same 368 tasks (eight per scenario, all play-out tasks). Jev [TypeSafe AI, 2026], decision model that picks among typed options without generating text, gets the same text with each task posed as choice over its candidates (Section E). Results. Table 4 and Figure 1 give four findings. The system the LLM agents built is the strongest player. TAVERNAGENT answers 91% of the play tasks; the best LLM playing directly, GPT-6 Astra, 63%, the Claude models 5253%, GPT-6.1 Sol 46%, Gemini 3.8 Flash 44% and the remaining models 2240%. It is near-perfect on combat, positioning, ordering and targets, where LLMs must simulate fights in their head; with TAVERNGYM as tool they recover most of that gap (GPT-6 Astra 62% to 97%, Table 15). Latency rules out live play for the LLMs. late recruit turn lasts about two minutes and holds up to about hundred operations, so decision that takes more than second cannot be played. TAVERNAGENT answers task in 0.03  (Table 4)  . Gateway timings are not comparable across providers, so we time every LLM on one standard footing [Artificial Analysis, 2026]: the median time to its first answer token, which includes the models typical thinking, plus the tasks answer at its median output speed. Their median task takes 1.426 s, DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash without reasoning 0.9 s. Within the one-second budget TAVERNAGENT keeps 90%, DeepSeek its 26% and Jev its 37%, and every other LLM falls to 0%. Speed alone would not suffice: turn chains dozens of decisions into one plan, so model that errs on third of them does not play third worse, it loses the plan; per-decision errors compound over turn rather than average out. Reading rules is not playing. The frontier LLMs execute rules well (GPT-6 Astra 95%, Claude Opus 92%, Gemini 3.8 Flash 90%), yet fall well short on the play tasks built from the same rules: knowing what each card does is not knowing which play wins. Judging game is not computing fight. On the turn plans scored by playing the game out, TAVERNAGENTs policy answers 75% in 0.03 s; the best LLM reaches 54% with seconds of reasoning, the others 1943%. Its policy also leads on the choices cut from natural games (81%).

sections.title: 8 Lessons from Self-Improvement
sections.content: The reality loop and the gates caught errors that no simulated metric revealed. We report six, each found and corrected inside the loop; four of them also changed the research process. (i) Copied games leak the future. search over game copies appeared to add 23.6 points of first-place rate; the copies carried the random-number state, so the search saw the real future shop and combat outcomes. Reseeded per sample, the gain vanished (0.65 1.14 points). (ii) Two errors can cancel. The exam once matched live results only because its late-game opponents were too strong while the agents growth was overstated; once both were fixed, the exam first-place rate rose to 4349%. (iii) Winners curse. The best of many snapshots overstated its gain (+1.22.1 points on selection seeds, 0.7 on unseen ones); hence gate G4. (iv) Calibrate to the opponents you meet. Measure library on the opponents the learner meets, not on uniform draws. (v) The ladder catches what simulation praises. TA-10 nearly doubled its predecessors exam first-place rate (24.2% against 12.8%), yet on the ladder the rating fell from 8,968 to 7,658 within 32 games, 18 of which also had client failures (Figure 3). The loop paused live testing, traced the fall to client failures and an earlyand mid-game weakness the exam had hidden, and retrained; TA-11 resumed the climb. (vi) Two encoders drift apart. Replays of live games showed the agent selling its whole warband on one turn far more often than in simulation; one input flag was encoded differently by the controller and the simulator after trinket choice. The fix added bit-level comparison of both encoders to gate G2.

sections.title: 9 Conclusion
sections.content: We presented AUTOTAVERN, self-improving research system: LLM research agents improve model, its training world and their own research process from the feedback of real environment, in closed loop of training, research and live games. In 20 days it built TAVERNGYM, faithful, full-content reproduction of Hearthstone Battlegrounds, and TAVERNAGENT, which plays complete games on the live ladder at the level of the servers best players. Asked to make the same decisions directly, frontier LLMs, including the models that built the system, fall well short of it and decide far too slowly for live turn: LLM agents build far better than they play. We will open-source TAVERNBENCH and TAVERNGYM at https://github.com/MCG-NJU/AutoTavern; limitations and ethics are discussed in Section D.

sections.title: A The AUTOTAVERN system in detail
sections.content: Conventions. Days count from day 1 of the project; all work targets patch 36.6.3. Agents. The research ran as several long-lived agent sessions inside our agentic research framework, each owning one role, plus short-lived sub-agents that session dispatched for probe, feature with its own test gate, or check.

sections.content: reads the memory, chooses the next problem, dispatches work, records findings implements rules and content, verifies rules, fixes discrepancies found in live games designs recipes and curricula, registers training runs and their successors builds and recalibrates the human-like opponent libraries evaluates within one build, re-checks candidates on unseen seeds, reviews maintains the client controller and the models input formats, collects live games short tasks: probes, features behind test gate, data analysis, reviews sets goals, rules on ambiguous mechanics, follows progress; in live games presses the shortcut key the AI names Shared research memory. All coordination goes through versioned text files: ledger of numbered findings (date, configuration, readings, conclusion; corrections are new entries that point back), registry of 220 confirmed rule decisions and list of open rule questions, hand-over note read at every change of hands, persistent memory of lessons loaded at the start of every session, and an experiment registry (about 10,000 experiments, each with its module, resources, priority, dependencies and successors). Fixes from live games. Over the 20 days, discrepancies that live games exposed led to 184 fixes, each underlying defect counted once: 35 of game rules and card behaviour in TAVERNGYM, and 11 of card data and offer rules read from client records; 73 of the input encoding, where the controller and the simulator described the same state differently; 51 of the client controller: reading the game state, executing operations, recovery; 14 recalibrations of the opponent libraries and exams to the opponents met in live games.

sections.title: B TAVERNGYM details
sections.content: Figure 4: TAVERNGYM. The Rust engine, its Python bindings and the programs built on them; the client controller feeds the live game to the agent in the same encoding. 12 Architecture. TAVERNGYM is Rust workspace of two crates: the game engine (about 63 thousand lines, of which 27 thousand are card scripts) and thin Python bindings whose batched calls release the interpreter lock. Recruit phase and combat share one effect context; every card is table of event hooks; the state is an arena of entities with integer identifiers that is cheap to copy and serialisable to JSON; all randomness comes from one seeded generator. source hash identifies every build and rule hash every rule set, and checkpoint trained under another rule hash is not resumed. Content. The card table is generated from the games data files; later patches are applied as an overlay. All 978 objects of patch 36.6.3 (minions, heroes and their Hero Powers, spells, trinkets and other cards) are implemented. Verification. Each mechanic was checked against the game data and official and community sources and the check recorded (375 records); confirmed rulings go to the decision registry (220) and unresolved ones to list of open questions. Every mechanic has unit test, and fuzzing plays random legal actions and checks state invariants after every action. RL interface. 245 discrete actions (end turn, refresh, freeze, upgrade, Hero Power, buy, sell, play or magnetize hand card to position, move minion, choose among offers), each with an exact legality mask. The observation contains only what the player sees, with opponents warbands as last seen in combat. batched environment runs many eight-player games at once, and running games can be saved and restored exactly. Performance. One core plays 190280 complete eight-player games per second with scripted bots and 5276 thousand late-game combats per second.

Libraries were first built from statistics of top human players (tribe shares, upgrade curves, purchase rates, warband strength by turn) and recorded games; each turn library seat takes an entry that matches target strength curve. sections.title: D Live deployment
sections.content: Setting and ethics. All games were played in the solo mode of the live game on the authors own account, without commercial purpose, on days 518 of the project. The controller feeds the live games state to the current TAVERNAGENT version in the environments own encoding; the AI decides every operation and names it, and human presses the shortcut key that performs that purchase, sale, play, choice or target, exactly as named, making no decision of their own. Shortcut keys and state-based hints are both features of the games official plug-in. When proposal was illegal in the client (an encoding or controller error), the game was abandoned and the error fixed before play resumed, so no human judgement enters the games counted. The study covers one game and one patch, with calibrated library opponents in training. Records. Each ladder result (392 games, read from the games history screens) is linked to the controllers decision logs, which name the model in play. The rating chain is continuous from 6,000 to 14,007; four results without recorded placement count in it but not in the placement statistics 16 (388 valid placements). Table 10 uses only the games that are linked with high confidence to single version, and Table 12 adds the games with client failure. The rating measures accumulated wins as much as strength: it rises only as fast as games are played, and the ladder was played for two weeks. We therefore compare recent results on one measure for every player: the public leaderboard tracker [wallii.gg, 2026] records each players rating updates and estimates placement for each from the rating change (a record can cover one or several games; ties are estimated as x.5). The estimate is the same for every player, so it compares players fairly even though it is not count of games; we do not mix it with our own logs, which the other players do not have. The agent met the same top players: in the 20 games whose opponents could be looked up on the leaderboard, the 29 opponents found were rated 12,19017,583 (median 13,294). The logged record ends at 14,007. The loop kept playing, and Table 11 compares the last 20 leaderboard records of every player at the cut-off, when the agent was rated about 15,000 and in the servers top 100. Its average placement, 1.60 with 80% first places, is better than that of each of the ten highest-rated players (1.883.03; 2.34 and 59% together), and its rating gain per record (+64) is nine times theirs (+7). On every statistic of this window the agent is ahead of the ten highest-rated players, and at the cut-off its rating was still rising steeply with no sign of plateau: it plays at the level of the servers best. sections.content: executed one-on-one executed / simulated simulated simulated simulated simulated human, simulated, play-out play-out purchase all all all all all all Scenes. Every static task starts from real game state that the environment reshapes for its scenario (turn, tier, gold, health, and warbands drawn from the current card pool by the scenarios filter), with heroes whose Hero Powers have no effect in the scene, so that no hidden effect changes label. Strategy and natural-choice tasks are instead cut from games of the main exam lobby  (Table 3)  at decisions of the kind. Labels and scoring. Rule tasks execute the stated actions on copies of the scene. task whose outcome involves random numbers is kept only when two or three reseeded copies agree. Combat tasks use 4,096 simulated combats (the damage-distribution scenario 400 single combats), and arrangement tasks 2,048 combats per arrangement. probability triple is correct when its most likely outcome matches and its Brier score is at most 0.1 (graded 1 Brier/2). Decision tasks label every option by 1,024 combats after it. task is kept when the choice matters: the best option beats the median one by 58 points of win rate, and at most quarter of the options are within three points of the best. An answer is correct when its option is within three points of the best, and its graded score is its win rate over the best ones. Strategy tasks are cut at the first decision of turn in natural games of the main-exam lobby. Four plans (upgrade the Tavern; buy the minion the labeller prefers; refresh first; end the turn and keep the Gold), each legal in the state, are each played out 128 times by the labeller (TA-21), which plays 18 the rest of the turn and the game as it sees fit. task is kept when the best plans mean placement beats the second-bests by 0.25 places and two standard errors of the difference, and the letters AD rotate so that each is the answer about equally often (chance 25%). Ending the turn is never the best plan; the contest is among the other three. The labels are outcomes of play, not the labelling agents preferences: answering with its own policy, the labeller (TA-21) reaches 73% on these tasks, the evaluated TA-23 75%, and the first version TA-1 57%. Hero and trinket tasks use the average placement of top human players in public statistics and keep offers whose best option leads by 0.1 (heroes) or 0.15 (trinkets) places. Prompts. One system prompt for all tasks; the user prompt has rules summary (economy, triples, combat order, keywords, damage), the player-visible state, the rule text of every card shown, the question with its objective and the JSON answer format. target task, abridged: Turn 6. All models were queried through their APIs with the benchmarks system prompt and no tools, streamed, within the output budget; where an API does not stop generation at the budget, answers over it are scored as cut off. Modes and budget. pilot with one task from each scenario chose each models mode: KimiK2.6, DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash and Intern-S2-Preview answer with reasoning off, the other models with low-effort reasoning. In the evaluation 48% of Grok 4.7s, 23% of Kimi-K2.6s and 16% of Gemini 3.8 Flashs answers were over the budget, at most 4% of the other models. Per task the LLMs used 0.93.9k input tokens and 92,772 output tokens (Grok 4.7: 6,625). Latency. Measured wall-clock times include queueing and start-up and depend on the access path, so the paper times every LLM on one standard footing (Section 7). tasks time is the median time to the first answer token of the models first-party API, in the variant that matches our setting, plus the tasks answer at the median output speed, both as published by Artificial Analysis [Artificial Analysis, 2026]. The first-answer time includes the models typical thinking; model without listing takes the medians of the listed ones. On our tasks some models think far longer than that: Grok 4.7 generates 19 3,600 tokens for the median task even at low effort. Timed with their own output tokens instead, the median task takes 350 s, and every real-time score stays the same. Decision model. Jev [TypeSafe AI, 2026] takes state and typed questions and returns, per question, the chosen option with probability for every option; it does not write free text. Its state is the prompts rules summary, player view and card rules, its instructions the tasks question, and every task is posed as choice over candidates: choice tasks: the options the task lists; target tasks: every warband or hand position; ordering tasks: every order of the listed actions (up to 24); purchase tasks: every purchase sequence the Gold allows (up to 157); probability tasks: win, tie and loss, or die and survive, whose probabilities are the answer; numeric tasks: the integers 030 for Gold and damage (the expected damage is the mean of its distribution) and 060 for each Attack and Health; legality tasks: legal or illegal for each action. The candidate lists hold every option and none of the labels values, and the common scorer applies. Jev answered every task without an error in 0.26 per task (median, one request per task) with 1.9k input tokens; its billed output tokens count option probabilities rather than generated text, so the output budget does not apply. Full set. On all 960 tasks TAVERNAGENT answers 92% of the play tasks, against 91% on the 368 tasks that every system answers. LLMs with TAVERNGYM as tool. To separate what the simulator contributes from what the policy contributes, five LLMs answered the short-term decision tasks (positioning, ordering, targets, purchases, discover and hand choices) with two tools over the tasks state in TAVERNGYM: test_play(actions) applies recruit actions in the engine and fights the next combat 256 times, TAVERNAGENTs budget per candidate, and inspect(actions) shows the resulting state; at most twelve calls per task, the same prompt otherwise. Table 15 compares each model with its own text-only answers on the same tasks. The tools close most of the gap to TAVERNAGENT, and the remainder is the models own: illegal or mis-indexed actions (hand positions shift after play), candidates left untested within the budget, and purchase sequences, where the candidate space is largest. Every model answered all 144 tasks (eight per scenario); Kimi-K2.6, Intern-S2-Preview and DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash ran with reasoning off, the others at low effort. sections.title: F Compute resources
sections.content: Main-line training ran on eight H200 GPUs with 128 CPU cores. Training the 23 delivered TAVERNAGENT stages took about 1,900 GPU-hours; all other training runs of the 20 days (explorations, ablations and abandoned lines) about 16,700 GPU-hours, and evaluations and analyses about 1,300 GPU-hours (from the experiment registry over the 20 days, every run counted at its configured size). The research agents ran on frontier LLMs, the GPT models GPT-6.1 Sol and GPT-6 Astra and Claude Opus 5.5, inside our agentic research framework, and together they generated about 100 million output tokens over the 20 days.
